name: Arcus tangent
seoDesc: Arcus tangent: a free math calculator that walks you through 4 values, with the formula spelled out and a worked example.
summary:
The Arcus tangent calculator returns your result from the 1 field on the form. No sign-up, no page reload, and the relationship behind it is printed below.

It suits a homework check, a spreadsheet build or a bit of mental arithmetic you want to confirm. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Arcus tangent calculator work?
sections.html:
The Arcus tangent calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationships described below and reports every result it can derive from them.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the figures it asks for.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html: • A plain number with no unit attached.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose x = 10. Working through the relationship above gives y = 84.2894 deg.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: y = 84.2894 deg should be roughly the size you expected from x = 10.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in degrees, and convertible to any of the 12 units on that chip.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Angle, opening in degrees

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Arcus tangent calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Building the same calculation into a spreadsheet and wanting a reference value
  • Settling an argument about a number with a quick, traceable result
  • Splitting a bill, a measurement or a shape problem between several people

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html: • Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the Arcus tangent calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The unit chips cover the units listed on the page. A historical or regional unit that is missing can still be used by converting it to a listed unit first.
  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

sections.title: How do you check the answer yourself?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time — X for instance — and watch which results move. A result that stays put does not depend on it.
  • Try a round value you can work out in your head. If the answer matches your mental arithmetic, the inputs are on the scale you assumed.
  • Switch the units to the ones you normally use and confirm the numbers are unchanged apart from their label; if they are not, a chip was on the wrong setting.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Arcus tangent calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for a few values, which is 1 field in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter Y in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Y opens in degrees and the chip beside it offers 12 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports y = 84.2894 deg. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Arcus tangent calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
